Loading, joining, cleaning, and validating the Olist dataset

Overview and Analytical Goal

To predict order delivery duration (delivery_days), I first assemble a single, analysis ready dataset. In this page, I load the six source tables, verify table dimensions and keys, merge them at the order item level, document every cleaning and missing data rule with row counts, run baseline sanity checks, and save the cleaned dataset for exploration in further steps.

Code 
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)

Step 1: Loading the Six Raw Olist Tables

Read the six raw CSV files (customers, category_translation, order_items, orders, products, and sellers)

Code 
customers <- read_csv("data/customers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
category_translation <- read_csv("data/category_translation.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

raw_table_summary <- tibble(
  table_name = c("order_items", "orders", "customers", "products", "sellers", "category_translation"),
  rows = c(nrow(order_items), nrow(orders), nrow(customers), nrow(products), nrow(sellers), nrow(category_translation)),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(orders), ncol(customers), ncol(products), ncol(sellers), ncol(category_translation)),
  primary_key = c("order_id + order_item_id", "order_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "seller_id", "product_category_name")
)

kable(
  raw_table_summary,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Table Name", "Row Count", "Column Count", "Join / Primary Key"),
  caption = "Dimensions and join keys of the six raw Olist tables"
)
Dimensions and join keys of the six raw Olist tables
Table Name Row Count Column Count Join / Primary Key
order_items 112,650 7 order_id + order_item_id
orders 99,441 11 order_id
customers 99,441 5 customer_id
products 32,951 9 product_id
sellers 3,095 4 seller_id
category_translation 71 2 product_category_name

order_items (112,650 rows) is more granular than orders (99,441 rows) because a single order can contain multiple items or sellers, making order_items the right base grain for item-level delivery analysis.

One row is one order at Olist website : one order, its customer, its order status, and its delivery days. The file holds 99441 rows and 11 columns, covering 99441 orders and 99441 customers.

Data dictionary

Column meanings for the six tables. Prices and freight are in Brazilian reais (BRL).

Customers table

Column Type Meaning
customer_id text Id per order; links an order to a customer record
customer_unique_id text Permanent id of a real customer
customer_zip_code_prefix number First 5 digits of the customer’s zip code
customer_city text Customer’s city
customer_state text Two-letter state code

Orders table (one row per order)

Column Type Meaning
order_id text Id of the order
customer_id text Links the order to the customers table
order_status text Status of the order (for example delivered or canceled)
order_purchase_timestamp datetime When the customer placed the order
purchase_year, purchase_month, purchase_day_of_week number / text Parts of the purchase timestamp
order_delivered_customer_date datetime When the customer received the order
order_estimated_delivery_date datetime Delivery date Olist estimated at checkout
delivery_days number Target. Whole days from purchase to delivery; missing when there is no delivery date
estimated_days number Whole days from purchase to Olist’s estimated delivery date

Order items table (one row per item in an order)

Column Type Meaning
order_id text Id of the order
order_item_id number Item position within the order
product_id text Id of the product
seller_id text Id of the seller
shipping_limit_date datetime Seller’s deadline to hand the item to the carrier
price number Item price in BRL
freight_value number Shipping cost in BRL

Products table

Column Type Meaning
product_id text Id of the product
product_category_name text Product category in Portuguese
product_name_lenght number Characters in the product name (spelled as in the raw file; renamed below)
product_description_lenght number Characters in the product description (renamed below)
product_photos_qty number Number of published photos
product_weight_g number Weight in grams
product_length_cm, product_height_cm, product_width_cm number Package dimensions in cm

Sellers table

Column Type Meaning
seller_id text Id of the seller
seller_zip_code_prefix number First 5 digits of the seller’s zip code
seller_city text Seller’s city
seller_state text Two-letter state code

Category translation table

Column Type Meaning
product_category_name text Category name in Portuguese
product_category_name_english text Category name in English

The full Olist dataset also has payments, reviews, and geolocation tables, which this project does not use. Review scores are written after delivery, so they cannot be used to predict it. Payments and geolocation were left out to keep the scope on what drives delivery time; real seller-to-customer distance from the geolocation table is the main next step noted on the Conclusion page.

Step 2: Joining the Six Tables into One Master Dataset

Starts from order_items and joins orders, customers, products, category_translation, and sellers via left_join(), comparing row counts before and after joining to verify there is no row multiplication.

Code 
rows_before_join <- nrow(order_items)

df_master <- order_items |>
  left_join(orders, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(customers, by = "customer_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  left_join(category_translation, by = "product_category_name") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id")

rows_after_join <- nrow(df_master)

join_check <- tibble(
  stage = c("Before joins (order_items)", "After joining all 6 tables (df_master)"),
  rows = c(rows_before_join, rows_after_join),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(df_master))
)

kable(
  join_check,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Pipeline Stage", "Row Count", "Column Count"),
  caption = "Row-count validation before and after merging the six Olist tables"
)
Row-count validation before and after merging the six Olist tables
Pipeline Stage Row Count Column Count
Before joins (order_items) 112,650 7
After joining all 6 tables (df_master) 112,650 33

Joining the six tables keeps 112,650 rows (matching 112,650 rows in order_items) across 33 columns, confirming zero row inflation during the merges.

Step 3: Auditing Missing Values and Cleaning Rules

Audits missing values across all columns of df_master, fixes column spelling typos, creates purchase_year_month, filters out rows missing delivery_days, and labels missing product categories as “unknown”. Missing numeric product fields are left as they are and filled later, inside the model recipe.

Code 
na_before <- tibble(
  column = names(df_master),
  missing_count = colSums(is.na(df_master)),
  missing_pct = round(100 * colSums(is.na(df_master)) / nrow(df_master), 2)
) |>
  filter(missing_count > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_count))

kable(
  na_before,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Column Name", "Missing Rows", "Missing Share (%)"),
  caption = "Columns with missing values in the raw joined dataset"
)
Columns with missing values in the raw joined dataset
Column Name Missing Rows Missing Share (%)

delivery_days 2,454 2.18
product_category_name_english 1,627 1.44
product_category_name 1,603 1.42
product_name_lenght 1,603 1.42
product_description_lenght 1,603 1.42
product_photos_qty 1,603 1.42
product_weight_g 18 0.02
product_length_cm 18 0.02

Code 
rows_initial <- nrow(df_master)
missing_del_n <- sum(is.na(df_master$delivery_days))

df_master <- df_master |>
  rename(
    product_name_length = product_name_lenght,
    product_description_length = product_description_lenght
  ) |>
  mutate(
    purchase_year_month = make_date(purchase_year, purchase_month, 1)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days))

rows_after_target_filter <- nrow(df_master)

df_master <- df_master |>
  mutate(
    # A missing category becomes its own level, so these items keep their route and timing records
    product_category_name = if_else(is.na(product_category_name), "unknown", product_category_name),
    product_category_name_english = if_else(
      is.na(product_category_name_english),
      product_category_name,
      product_category_name_english
    )
  )

# Numeric product fields that can still be missing. They are NOT filled here: a median computed
# on the full dataset would use the future test rows, so the fill happens inside the model recipe
product_num_cols <- c("product_name_length", "product_description_length", "product_photos_qty",
                      "product_weight_g", "product_length_cm", "product_height_cm", "product_width_cm")

na_after <- tibble(
  column = names(df_master),
  missing_count = colSums(is.na(df_master)),
  missing_pct = round(100 * colSums(is.na(df_master)) / nrow(df_master), 2)
) |>
  filter(missing_count > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_count))

kable(
  na_after,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Column Name", "Missing Rows", "Missing Share (%)"),
  caption = "Columns that still have missing values after cleaning (all numeric product fields)"
)
Columns that still have missing values after cleaning (all numeric product fields)
Column Name Missing Rows Missing Share (%)
product_name_length 1,537 1.39
product_description_length 1,537 1.39
product_photos_qty 1,537 1.39
product_weight_g 18 0.02
product_length_cm 18 0.02
product_height_cm 18 0.02
product_width_cm 18 0.02
Code 
n_rows_missing_spec <- sum(!complete.cases(df_master[product_num_cols]))

Summary of Cleaning Decisions (One Sentence per Rule)

  • Column name & date standardization: Corrected the raw typos (product_name_lenght -> product_name_length and product_description_lenght -> product_description_length) and built purchase_year_month so naming is consistent and monthly trends can be tracked cleanly.
  • Missing target removal: Removed 2,454 rows (2.18%) missing delivery_days—moving from 112,650 to 110,196 rows—because records without an observed delivery duration cannot train or evaluate a delivery_days model.
  • Category missingness ("unknown"): Filled missing product_category_name and product_category_name_english entries with "unknown" rather than dropping rows so uncategorized items still contribute shipping, timing, and geographic records.
  • Numeric product fields left missing, filled later: The seven numeric product specification columns (product_name_length, product_description_length, product_photos_qty, product_weight_g, product_length_cm, product_height_cm, and product_width_cm) still have missing values in 1,538 rows. They are not imputed here. A median calculated on the whole dataset would use information from rows that later become the test set, so the Modeling page fills them with the median of the training rows only, inside the recipe. The exploration pages simply ignore the missing values when they compute summaries.

After cleaning, 4,683 missing values remain, all in the numeric product fields listed above, across 34 columns and 110,196 rows (96,476 unique orders).

Step 4: Baseline Sanity Checks (Status, Target Summary, Timing, and Geography)

Checks order statuses and cancellation rate, overall delivery_days statistics, purchase day/month coverage, and seller-state delivery patterns before moving to exploration.

4.1: Order Status and Cancellation Rate

Code 
status_summary <- df_master |>
  count(order_status, name = "order_item_rows") |>
  mutate(
    pct_rows = round(100 * order_item_rows / sum(order_item_rows), 4)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(order_item_rows))

kable(
  status_summary,
  digits = 4,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Order Status", "Order-Item Rows", "Share (%)"),
  caption = "Order-item rows and percentage share by order status"
)
Order-item rows and percentage share by order status
Order Status Order-Item Rows Share (%)
delivered 110,189 99.9936
canceled 7 0.0064

Among rows with a recorded delivery_days value, "canceled" rows represent only 7 rows (0.0064% cancellation rate), showing that cancellations are rare once delivery dates are present.

Step 5: Saving the Cleaned Dataset and Next Step

Saves the cleaned df_master dataset to data/df_master_clean.rds so downstream pages load a consistent, validated dataset. The numeric product fields are still unfilled at this point.

With df_master_clean.rds saved, the Exploration page examines delivery_days directly first, then tests relationships across geography, purchase month, shipping cost, and product characteristics before closing with a data backed decision and limitations.

Source Code
---
title: "Data"
subtitle: "Loading, joining, cleaning, and validating the Olist dataset"
---

## Overview and Analytical Goal
 To predict order delivery duration (`delivery_days`), I first assemble a single, analysis ready dataset. In this page, I load the six source tables, verify table dimensions and keys, merge them at the order item level, document every cleaning and missing data rule with row counts, run baseline sanity checks, and save the cleaned dataset for exploration in further steps.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)
```

## Step 1: Loading the Six Raw Olist Tables
 Read the six raw CSV files (customers, category_translation, order_items, orders, products, and sellers)

```{r}
customers <- read_csv("data/customers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
category_translation <- read_csv("data/category_translation.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

raw_table_summary <- tibble(
  table_name = c("order_items", "orders", "customers", "products", "sellers", "category_translation"),
  rows = c(nrow(order_items), nrow(orders), nrow(customers), nrow(products), nrow(sellers), nrow(category_translation)),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(orders), ncol(customers), ncol(products), ncol(sellers), ncol(category_translation)),
  primary_key = c("order_id + order_item_id", "order_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "seller_id", "product_category_name")
)

kable(
  raw_table_summary,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Table Name", "Row Count", "Column Count", "Join / Primary Key"),
  caption = "Dimensions and join keys of the six raw Olist tables"
)
```

`order_items` (`r format(nrow(order_items), big.mark = ",")` rows) is more granular than `orders` (`r format(nrow(orders), big.mark = ",")` rows) because a single order can contain multiple items or sellers, making `order_items` the right base grain for item-level delivery analysis.

One row is one order at Olist website : one order, its customer, its order status, and its delivery days. The file holds `r nrow(orders)` rows and `r ncol(orders)` columns, covering `r n_distinct(orders$order_id)` orders and `r n_distinct(orders$customer_id)` customers.

```{r}
glimpse(customers)
glimpse(category_translation)
glimpse(order_items)
glimpse(orders)
glimpse(products)
glimpse(sellers)
```

## Data dictionary

Column meanings for the six tables. Prices and freight are in Brazilian reais (BRL).

**Customers table**

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `customer_id` | text | Id per order; links an order to a customer record |
| `customer_unique_id` | text | Permanent id of a real customer |
| `customer_zip_code_prefix` | number | First 5 digits of the customer's zip code |
| `customer_city` | text | Customer's city |
| `customer_state` | text | Two-letter state code |

**Orders table** (one row per order)

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `order_id` | text | Id of the order |
| `customer_id` | text | Links the order to the customers table |
| `order_status` | text | Status of the order (for example delivered or canceled) |
| `order_purchase_timestamp` | datetime | When the customer placed the order |
| `purchase_year`, `purchase_month`, `purchase_day_of_week` | number / text | Parts of the purchase timestamp |
| `order_delivered_customer_date` | datetime | When the customer received the order |
| `order_estimated_delivery_date` | datetime | Delivery date Olist estimated at checkout |
| `delivery_days` | number | **Target.** Whole days from purchase to delivery; missing when there is no delivery date |
| `estimated_days` | number | Whole days from purchase to Olist's estimated delivery date |

**Order items table** (one row per item in an order)

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `order_id` | text | Id of the order |
| `order_item_id` | number | Item position within the order |
| `product_id` | text | Id of the product |
| `seller_id` | text | Id of the seller |
| `shipping_limit_date` | datetime | Seller's deadline to hand the item to the carrier |
| `price` | number | Item price in BRL |
| `freight_value` | number | Shipping cost in BRL |

**Products table**

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `product_id` | text | Id of the product |
| `product_category_name` | text | Product category in Portuguese |
| `product_name_lenght` | number | Characters in the product name (spelled as in the raw file; renamed below) |
| `product_description_lenght` | number | Characters in the product description (renamed below) |
| `product_photos_qty` | number | Number of published photos |
| `product_weight_g` | number | Weight in grams |
| `product_length_cm`, `product_height_cm`, `product_width_cm` | number | Package dimensions in cm |

**Sellers table**

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `seller_id` | text | Id of the seller |
| `seller_zip_code_prefix` | number | First 5 digits of the seller's zip code |
| `seller_city` | text | Seller's city |
| `seller_state` | text | Two-letter state code |

**Category translation table**

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `product_category_name` | text | Category name in Portuguese |
| `product_category_name_english` | text | Category name in English |

The full Olist dataset also has payments, reviews, and geolocation tables, which this project does not use. Review scores are written after delivery, so they cannot be used to predict it. Payments and geolocation were left out to keep the scope on what drives delivery time; real seller-to-customer distance from the geolocation table is the main next step noted on the Conclusion page.

## Step 2: Joining the Six Tables into One Master Dataset
Starts from `order_items` and joins `orders`, `customers`, `products`, `category_translation`, and `sellers` via `left_join()`, comparing row counts before and after joining to verify there is no row multiplication.

```{r}
rows_before_join <- nrow(order_items)

df_master <- order_items |>
  left_join(orders, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(customers, by = "customer_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  left_join(category_translation, by = "product_category_name") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id")

rows_after_join <- nrow(df_master)

join_check <- tibble(
  stage = c("Before joins (order_items)", "After joining all 6 tables (df_master)"),
  rows = c(rows_before_join, rows_after_join),
  columns = c(ncol(order_items), ncol(df_master))
)

kable(
  join_check,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Pipeline Stage", "Row Count", "Column Count"),
  caption = "Row-count validation before and after merging the six Olist tables"
)
```
 Joining the six tables keeps `r format(rows_after_join, big.mark = ",")` rows (matching `r format(rows_before_join, big.mark = ",")` rows in `order_items`) across `r ncol(df_master)` columns, confirming zero row inflation during the merges.


## Step 3: Auditing Missing Values and Cleaning Rules
Audits missing values across all columns of `df_master`, fixes column spelling typos, creates `purchase_year_month`, filters out rows missing `delivery_days`, and labels missing product categories as "unknown". Missing numeric product fields are left as they are and filled later, inside the model recipe.

```{r}
na_before <- tibble(
  column = names(df_master),
  missing_count = colSums(is.na(df_master)),
  missing_pct = round(100 * colSums(is.na(df_master)) / nrow(df_master), 2)
) |>
  filter(missing_count > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_count))

kable(
  na_before,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Column Name", "Missing Rows", "Missing Share (%)"),
  caption = "Columns with missing values in the raw joined dataset"
)
```

```{r}
rows_initial <- nrow(df_master)
missing_del_n <- sum(is.na(df_master$delivery_days))

df_master <- df_master |>
  rename(
    product_name_length = product_name_lenght,
    product_description_length = product_description_lenght
  ) |>
  mutate(
    purchase_year_month = make_date(purchase_year, purchase_month, 1)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days))

rows_after_target_filter <- nrow(df_master)

df_master <- df_master |>
  mutate(
    # A missing category becomes its own level, so these items keep their route and timing records
    product_category_name = if_else(is.na(product_category_name), "unknown", product_category_name),
    product_category_name_english = if_else(
      is.na(product_category_name_english),
      product_category_name,
      product_category_name_english
    )
  )

# Numeric product fields that can still be missing. They are NOT filled here: a median computed
# on the full dataset would use the future test rows, so the fill happens inside the model recipe
product_num_cols <- c("product_name_length", "product_description_length", "product_photos_qty",
                      "product_weight_g", "product_length_cm", "product_height_cm", "product_width_cm")

na_after <- tibble(
  column = names(df_master),
  missing_count = colSums(is.na(df_master)),
  missing_pct = round(100 * colSums(is.na(df_master)) / nrow(df_master), 2)
) |>
  filter(missing_count > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_count))

kable(
  na_after,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Column Name", "Missing Rows", "Missing Share (%)"),
  caption = "Columns that still have missing values after cleaning (all numeric product fields)"
)

n_rows_missing_spec <- sum(!complete.cases(df_master[product_num_cols]))
```

### Summary of Cleaning Decisions (One Sentence per Rule)
* **Column name & date standardization:** Corrected the raw typos (`product_name_lenght` -> `product_name_length` and `product_description_lenght` -> `product_description_length`) and built `purchase_year_month` so naming is consistent and monthly trends can be tracked cleanly.
* **Missing target removal:** Removed `r format(missing_del_n, big.mark = ",")` rows (`r round(100 * missing_del_n / rows_initial, 2)`%) missing `delivery_days`—moving from `r format(rows_initial, big.mark = ",")` to `r format(rows_after_target_filter, big.mark = ",")` rows—because records without an observed delivery duration cannot train or evaluate a `delivery_days` model.
* **Category missingness (`"unknown"`):** Filled missing `product_category_name` and `product_category_name_english` entries with `"unknown"` rather than dropping rows so uncategorized items still contribute shipping, timing, and geographic records.
* **Numeric product fields left missing, filled later:** The seven numeric product specification columns (`product_name_length`, `product_description_length`, `product_photos_qty`, `product_weight_g`, `product_length_cm`, `product_height_cm`, and `product_width_cm`) still have missing values in `r format(n_rows_missing_spec, big.mark = ",")` rows. They are not imputed here. A median calculated on the whole dataset would use information from rows that later become the test set, so the Modeling page fills them with the median of the training rows only, inside the recipe. The exploration pages simply ignore the missing values when they compute summaries.

After cleaning, `r format(sum(colSums(is.na(df_master))), big.mark = ",")` missing values remain, all in the numeric product fields listed above, across `r ncol(df_master)` columns and `r format(nrow(df_master), big.mark = ",")` rows (`r format(n_distinct(df_master$order_id), big.mark = ",")` unique orders).


## Step 4: Baseline Sanity Checks (Status, Target Summary, Timing, and Geography)
Checks order statuses and cancellation rate, overall `delivery_days` statistics, purchase day/month coverage, and seller-state delivery patterns before moving to exploration.

### 4.1: Order Status and Cancellation Rate


```{r}
status_summary <- df_master |>
  count(order_status, name = "order_item_rows") |>
  mutate(
    pct_rows = round(100 * order_item_rows / sum(order_item_rows), 4)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(order_item_rows))

kable(
  status_summary,
  digits = 4,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Order Status", "Order-Item Rows", "Share (%)"),
  caption = "Order-item rows and percentage share by order status"
)
```
Among rows with a recorded `delivery_days` value, `"canceled"` rows represent only `r status_summary$order_item_rows[status_summary$order_status == "canceled"]` rows (`r status_summary$pct_rows[status_summary$order_status == "canceled"]`% cancellation rate), showing that cancellations are rare once delivery dates are present.

### 4.2: Overall delivery_days Summary

```{r}
overall_del_summary <- df_master |>
  summarise(
    min_days = min(delivery_days),
    avg_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_days = sd(delivery_days),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id)
  )

kable(
  overall_del_summary,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Min Days", "Mean Days", "Median Days", "Max Days", "SD Days", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Baseline summary statistics for delivery_days across cleaned orders"
)
```

Across `r format(overall_del_summary$num_orders, big.mark = ",")` orders, `delivery_days` has a mean of `r round(overall_del_summary$avg_days, 2)` days and a median of `r round(overall_del_summary$median_days, 2)` days (ranging from `r round(overall_del_summary$min_days, 1)` to `r round(overall_del_summary$max_days, 1)` days, SD = `r round(overall_del_summary$sd_days, 2)`), showing right skew from long tail deliveries.


### 4.3: Order Volume and Delivery Time by Day of Week and Purchase Span

```{r}
weekday_summary <- df_master |>
  group_by(purchase_day_of_week) |>
  summarise(
    avg_days = mean(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(num_orders))

kable(
  weekday_summary,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Purchase Day", "Mean Days", "Max Days", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Order volume and delivery duration by purchase day of week"
)

date_range_summary <- df_master |>
  summarise(
    min_month = min(purchase_year_month),
    max_month = max(purchase_year_month),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id)
  )

kable(
  date_range_summary,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Earliest Month", "Latest Month", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Purchase date coverage in the cleaned dataset"
)
```
The cleaned data spans `r date_range_summary$min_month` to `r date_range_summary$max_month` across `r format(date_range_summary$num_orders, big.mark = ",")` unique orders, with higher order counts on weekdays than weekends and mean `delivery_days` staying within a narrow band across days of the week.



### 4.4: Delivery Performance by Seller State

```{r}
seller_state_summary <- df_master |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    avg_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_days = median(delivery_days),
    min_days = min(delivery_days),
    max_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_days = sd(delivery_days),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_days))

kable(
  seller_state_summary,
  digits = 2,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Seller State", "Mean Days", "Median Days", "Min Days", "Max Days", "SD Days", "Unique Orders"),
  caption = "Delivery days and order volume by seller state (full width)"
)
```

Seller fulfillment is heavily concentrated in `SP` (`r format(seller_state_summary$num_orders[seller_state_summary$seller_state == "SP"], big.mark = ",")` orders), while states with slower averages such as `AM` (`r round(seller_state_summary$avg_days[seller_state_summary$seller_state == "AM"], 1)` mean days) represent small order counts (`r seller_state_summary$num_orders[seller_state_summary$seller_state == "AM"]` orders)—meaning state-level averages on tiny sample sizes need careful interpretation when modeling.

## Step 5: Saving the Cleaned Dataset and Next Step
Saves the cleaned `df_master` dataset to `data/df_master_clean.rds` so downstream pages load a consistent, validated dataset. The numeric product fields are still unfilled at this point.

```{r}
#| include: false
write_rds(df_master, "data/df_master_clean.rds")
```

With `df_master_clean.rds` saved, the **Exploration** page examines `delivery_days` directly first, then tests relationships across geography, purchase month, shipping cost, and product characteristics before closing with a data backed decision and limitations.
